readerMoment: Wants to build a home security lab and is excited about the tools. Has not thought about whose traffic the lab would see, or what it is actually for.
outcome: Can write a one-page scope for their lab: the devices and traffic they may observe, and the one failure they most want to catch.

teachingShape.realTask: Write the scope for your own lab before plugging anything in
activate: Lockout/tagout: you mark what is safe to work on before you touch it
A security camera pointed at your own driveway, not the neighbor's window
demonstrate: One complete worked scope for an example shared household, including its one failure to catch
apply: Reader picks the one failure they care about most
Reader fills in their own scope
integrate: The scope becomes the boundary of the lab built later in the series
Filling in devices needs a map of the network, which is the next page

requiredIdeas: Consent defines the lab. Owning the network does not give you authority over everyone's traffic on it.
In scope: devices you own or are explicitly allowed to watch. Out of scope: everyone else's, including devices on your Wi-Fi.
Metadata still says things about people, so it needs the same care.
A threat model is three questions: what you protect, from whom, and which failure you most want to catch.
Pick one failure to catch first. It decides what the lab watches.
Write the scope down before any tool is installed.
candidateAnalogies: Lockout/tagout before working on a machine
House keys: you already decide who gets access to what

deliberatelyExcluded.what: Legal advice for a specific place
deliberatelyExcluded.why: Laws vary. The page states the principle and points to sources.
Three questions are enough for a home lab. A framework is weight the reader doesn't need yet.
Different authority questions. Out of scope for a home lab.

nextPagePressure: To list the devices in scope, the reader needs to see how the home network is wired.
